title: American Airlines 6780
summary: On 22 January 1952, American Airlines Flight 6780, a Convair 240, was on final approach to Newark Airport using the instrument landing system when it crashed into a house in Elizabeth, New Jersey, approximately 3.4 miles southwest of Newark. The aircraft had gone 2,100 feet off course to the right. All 23 occupants on board plus 7 people on the ground were killed. The cause of the crash was never determined.

title: Pan Am 526A
summary: Pan Am Flight 526A ditched in the Atlantic Ocean after both engines lost power shortly after takeoff from San Juan. Engine number 3 failed at 350 feet and engine number 4 failed at 550 feet. The investigation revealed inadequate maintenance: engine 3 had not been changed when metal shavings were found in the engine oil, leading to its failure immediately after takeoff. The crew performed a water landing, but survivors panicked and refused to board life rafts, resulting in 52 deaths.
probable_cause: Engine number 3 was not changed when metal shavings were found in the engine oil in maintenance before this flight, leading to its failure immediately subsequent to take-off. The pilots' attempt to re-establish a climb without using all available power after the loss of power from the second engine led to a nose high pitch attitude and rapid decrease of airspeed.

title: Pan Am 202
summary: A Boeing 377 Stratocruiser registered N1039V, christened Clipper Good Hope, was operating an international scheduled passenger flight from Rio de Janeiro to Port of Spain, the third leg of a four-leg journey from Buenos Aires. The aircraft departed Rio at 2:43 a.m. on April 29, 1952 and was last heard from at 6:16 a.m. reporting abeam the city of Barreiras in eastern Brazil at 14,500 feet. It was expected to report abeam Carolina at 7:45 a.m. but the aircraft never reported again. Investigation of the wreckage found evidence indicating the No. 2 engine and propeller had failed in flight, causing the aircraft to break apart. It crashed in the dense Amazon jungle approximately 281 nautical miles southwest of Carolina. All 50 people aboard were killed.
probable_cause: The exact cause of the crash was not established. However, investigation of wreckage indicated that an engine had likely separated in flight after propeller blade failure, with the propeller failure causing the engine to experience highly unbalanced loads that eventually caused separation from the aircraft.

factors.evidence: evidence on the port wing root, the No. 2 engine nacelle, the leading edge of the vertical stabilizer, and the horizontal stabilizer led investigators to believe that the engine and/or propeller had failed in flight
the engine separation would have precipitated loss of control
the propeller failure caused the engine to experience highly unbalanced loads and it eventually separated from the aircraft, precipitating an in-flight breakup
a huge fire had consumed the fuselage

events.text: Flight 202 departed Rio de Janeiro at 2:43 a.m. on April 29, 1952 on an off-airways route directly to Port of Spain over the Amazon jungle
At 6:16 a.m. local time the flight reported abeam the city of Barreiras in eastern Brazil, flying at 14,500 feet under VFR conditions
The aircraft failed to report abeam Carolina at the estimated time of 7:45 a.m. as expected, and then failed to report abeam the city of Santarém in northern Brazil
Local authorities initiated a missing aircraft alert when all subsequent position reports failed to arrive

A properly equipped investigation team finally reached the wreckage on August 15, finding it had fallen to the ground in three main sections across dense forest 13 nautical miles northwest of their base camp, confirming all on board had died on impact and a huge fire had consumed the fuselage

notes: Exact cause not established due to difficult terrain and investigation conditions; propeller failure and engine separation is theorized based on wreckage examination

title: 1952 Moses Lake C-124 crash
summary: A United States Air Force Douglas C-124 Globemaster II transport aircraft carrying 105 passengers and 10 crew departed Larson Air Force Base near Moses Lake, Washington on December 20, 1952 as part of Operation Sleigh Ride to bring servicemen home from Korea. Just seconds after taking off, the left wing struck the ground and the aircraft cartwheeled, broke up and exploded. Investigation revealed the elevator and rudder gust locks had not been disengaged prior to departure.
probable_cause: The aircraft's elevator and rudder gust locks had not been disengaged prior to departure, causing loss of control during takeoff.

factors.evidence: The aircraft's elevator and rudder gust locks had not been disengaged prior to departure.
Just seconds after taking off, the left wing struck the ground and the aircraft cartwheeled.
The aircraft broke up and exploded.

events.text: C-124 lifted off from Larson Air Force Base near Moses Lake bound for Kelly Air Force Base in San Antonio, Texas.
Just seconds after taking off, left wing struck the ground causing aircraft to cartwheel.
Aircraft broke up and exploded, killing 82 of 105 passengers and 5 of 10 crew.
